I have a note from one of you. I'll deal with that. The answer is, yes, it'll be accommodated, just to reassure you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

But that has prompted me to say that we will address the issue of the rail strikes that are coming up. Unfortunately, trains do seem to be getting cancelled rather than a lot at the moment.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord, the witness [Nurse B] is in the witness box. Could she be sworn, please?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B (sworn)
Examination-in-chief by MR DRIVER

Please sit down. All right? You'll be being asked questions, as you know, from there. Try and keep your voice up, please. The microphone won't cause your voice to be amplified to the jury. Your natural voice has to carry around
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: the room. If you want a break at any time, just ask for a break, all right?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Could you tell the members of the jury your full name, please?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: [Nurse B].
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: [Nurse B], could you inform the jury as to your occupational status back in June 2015?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes. So I was a band 6 neonatal nurse at the Countess of Chester Hospital at that date, and that basically means I was a shift leader.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: In a very short while I'm going to be asking you questions that directly relate to the baby and patient, [Baby C], but before doing so, I'd like to invite you to expand a little more about your role within the unit at that time.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You told the jury moments ago that you were a band 6 nurse and a shift leader. Does it follow that every band 6 nurse is a shift leader or not?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: On our neonatal unit, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: As of June 2015 for how long approximately had you been a band 6 and a shift leader?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: A few years. I can't remember, I'm sorry.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's more than sufficient. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: As a shift leader on any particular shift, would you be designated the responsibility of caring for a specific baby or babies?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: When I was the shift leader?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: So ideally, no. The shift leader is ideally supernumerary, so that means that you oversee the care given to all of the babies. At times when it is extremely busy you may be allocated a baby, but ideally, no. You would cover breaks, so you would be -- you would be -- allocate breaks to cover them, but you wouldn't be allocated them for the duration of the shift unless necessary.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. So you'd be performing some sort of overseeing role?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: For the whole unit?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And for all the nurses and all the babies?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Prior to the commencement of a shift, what, if any, contribution would a shift leader make to the allocation of particular babies to particular nurses?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: So you would allocate the babies according to their requirements, whether that -- that depends on the level of care that they need. So it depends on the care of the baby, so whether they're transitional care, special care, high dependency or intensive care. And then it depends on the qualifications of the staff member. So an ITU baby -- do you want me to say -would be one nurse to one baby. Then the lower the care, the more babies allocated to one nurse.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. That answer you gave me had a number of parts to it, so if I can just retrace through that answer. Does it follow that shift leader has the responsibility for the allocation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You exercise some professional judgment --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- and you deem which nurses will look after which babies?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: But in order to reach such decisions, you apply certain guidance --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- and certain criteria? And that criteria takes into account, you told us, firstly the individual nurse's qualification and experience?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And on the other side of the equation, the particular babies' --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- needs. As to that criteria, do you receive that guidance externally? Is there a national standard?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: We will be following BAPM standards.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: BAPM being?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: BAPM -- oh gosh, you're testing me.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is it the British Association --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: British Association of Perinatal Medicine.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. I should have been in there earlier to help you. Apologies.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So they provide a standard --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- a set of guidelines?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: A set of guidelines for the baby, but obviously, as a shift leader, you know the staff individually.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That anticipated my next question: are those guidelines applied rigidly, without deviation at all?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: They will depend on staffing levels.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. And anything else?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: And the staffing that you have at that time on shift.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. As for the baby, how is the baby's status defined? For example, an intensive care baby, how is that defined?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: So that is very much defined by BAPM.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: So an example would be a baby on a ventilator, receiving ventilatory support, would be classed as intensive care, which will be ideally one-to-one nursing.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And a high dependency baby, what qualifies a baby to attract that status?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Again, many different things, but an example would be a baby on CPAP, respiratory support, but with peripheral venous access, not central access.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And to go down the scale one more stage, a special care baby?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Would be a baby that isn't receiving any additional breathing support, but that doesn't include supplementary oxygen which would be either in the incubator in the ambient space or from nasal prongs but no additional ventilation needs.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Moving away from the babies and nurses and just looking at the unit itself for a moment, we have already been informed that, as of June 2015, the Countess of Chester neonatal unit was what's deemed a level 2 unit.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And it follows, does it, that again there'd be certain criteria which would ideally be applied that govern whether a baby should be ideally delivered at the unit and, if so, kept at the unit?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And you would be familiar with that criteria?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Let's move from the general to the specific now if you would. I'm going to ask you about the shifts that you led that involved the care of [Baby C], who the jury know was born at 15.31 hours on 10 June 2015.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Rest assured, [Nurse B], if you're asked questions about the detail of his care, that screen in front of you will assist as to detail and nursing records.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You made a witness statement in relation to these proceedings on 13 February 2018. Prior to doing so, were you afforded the opportunity of reminding yourself of the contents of the nursing notes --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- in relation to baby [Baby C]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Independent of those notes, do you have a memory, do you recall some or all of the events?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Some, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Did you ever have direct responsibility for the hands-on designated care of [Baby C]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: No, I didn't.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: But were you a shift leader during the time when your colleagues did?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And did you direct or designate his care in the way that you've already described generally to the jury?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: So during the shift I was overseeing the care but I do not whether I allocated the nurse to him because back in 2015, around that time, we changed the system of who allocated. So today, we allocate the shift before.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So say for instance this shift in question we're talking about is a night shift, the day shift would now allocate for the night staff coming in.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: However, around that time, we changed, so I'm not sure I allocated [Baby C]'s nurse on this night because it was around that time we changed and it was the shift leader coming on that shift that night, who would have been me, that allocated. So the allocation may have already been done when I came in.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I understand. And when you refer to that night, I think you're talking about the shift, the night shift, that began on the evening of 13 June and went overnight into 14 June. Just to remind the jury, [Baby C]'s death, tragically, was timed at 05.58 hours on 14 June. So very much the shift that you were alluding to, I think.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You were working as shift leader on that night shift; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Do you recall who was designated as [Baby C]'s nurse?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And it was?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Sophie.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sophie Ellis?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: But does it flow from what you told us a minute or two ago, you can't be certain whether you selected that designation --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- or whether you inherited it --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- in effect? But whichever it was, would you have applied your mind to the appropriateness of that designation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes. Sophie was my former student, she was a very competent nurse.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. So when you say she was your former student, could you elaborate on that a little?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Sorry, yes. So when Sophie was in her training, she came through the neonatal unit as a student nurse on a placement and I was her mentor during the placement.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So I was the one overseeing her during her training, during that placement.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Which training and placement had concluded prior to --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- June 2015 and the jury have heard evidence from Sophie Ellis and they will recall that at this point she was a band 5 nurse. Does that accord with your recollection?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Was she fresh out of training at that point in time, do you recall?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: I don't recall exactly where she was, but she had -- Chester wasn't her first job after qualification, she had some level 3 unit experience.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The jury have heard that such units are designated into three tiers: local units being a level 1, places like Chester level 2, and tertiary, level 3. And at this point in time for your area that would have been Alder Hey or -- sorry, that would have been Liverpool Women's Hospital or Arrowe Park?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: In our network, yes. I don't think she was in the network.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Do you happen to know where she was elsewhere?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: I think it was Manchester or Leeds.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: In any event that was at a level 3 unit?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And what if any significance did you attach to that at that time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: That she was familiar with caring for babies such as [Baby C].
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Right. Let's focus on [Baby C] for a moment then.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Babies such as [Baby C]", what do you mean by that in this context?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Requiring the level of support, the size he was.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So [Baby C] was, as of 13 June, an intensive care baby?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And you've alluded to his size. We know he was born at about a weight of about 800 grams.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Which others have already told us that for his gestational age was deemed light.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is that a fact that you would have taken into account --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: I would, yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- at the time? Other than that, what if anything did you inform yourself about the general condition of baby [Baby C] when you took over as leader of that shift?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: So like at the start of any shift, I receive a full handover and I'll do a general walk around, not necessarily read into too much detail about each baby at that stage, just a general walk around. And from looking at the monitor that [Baby C] was attached to, and looking a quick glance at the charts, everything seemed stable. I had no concerns at the start of the shift.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: When you say stable, do you mean clinically stable?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Clinically, his observations were stable.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. He was in nursery room 1?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We understand. From your oversight of the unit on this shift, do you recall whether he was alone there or whether there was other baby or babies within that room?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: There was one more baby in that room.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Was Sophie Ellis designated for both babies or just for [Baby C]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Just for [Baby C].
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And do you recall who else was nursing in that room?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes, Melanie Taylor.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: In terms of your assessment of Melanie Taylor's level of experience and qualification, could you describe that to the jury, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes. Melanie is also a band 6 nurse, an experienced band 6 nurse, so the allocation being, whether it was my allocation or the shift before, the band 6 that will have also been a considering factor for -- if I wasn't available to be in the same nursery all the time with Sophie, then Mel would be there for support for Sophie.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And that's something that you took into account at the time, is it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You told us about the change in practice as to who was given responsibility of designating the nurses. You can't say whether or not you designated [Baby C] to Sophie Ellis or vice versa?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: I can't.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If not you, would you be able to say who it would have been?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: The shift leader on the day shift.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And at this distance in time you can't remember?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: No.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So Melanie Taylor was in the same room as Sophie Ellis and [Baby C], with another baby, and you were there to oversee the whole unit?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. We also know that nurse Lucy Letby was on duty during that night shift.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Do you recall which baby she was allocated to and, if so, please don't say the baby's name, but do you recall?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: I recall one baby. I think there were more, but I do definitely recall one.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: In which nursery was the baby that you recall?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Nursery 3.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could you tell us that baby's initials, if you remember them?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: JE.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: JE. Thank you. What is it about JE that causes you to recall that baby?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: So at the start of the shift, when I was doing my general walk around and becoming familiar with the babies, this particular baby, baby JE, I was familiar with and I was concerned about -- he had some signs of respiratory distress.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. When you say you were familiar with JE, could you expand upon how you were familiar with him?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: So I had been on shift when that baby was in the unit prior and I think I'd been his designated nurse, if not a shift leader, I was -- he had definitely been there a time period, I don't remember how long. But I remember noting straightaway his breathing status at the start of that shift was not as I remembered it.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Right. Had it improved or deteriorated?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Deteriorated.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What informed you of that, what data or what symptoms informed you?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: He was grunting, which is loud audible noise on expiration.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And had you previously noted that within baby JE?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Not when I had cared for him or seen him prior.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Was that an alert to you as the shift leader?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What did that prompt you to want to do for that baby?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: So I asked Lucy to increase his observations, charted observations, from two-hourly to one-hourly so we could make a proper assessment and see a trend in the data.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: And asked Lucy to call the registrar on call to come and review him immediately.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. And he, baby JE, was housed in nursery number 3, and from the hierarchical description you gave us earlier, it may be thought that a baby in nursery 1 necessarily would require more intensive observations than a baby in nursery 3. Is that overly simplistic or is that right?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: That could be true, but depending on the busyness of the ward, even a baby that is very close to discharge out in one of the nurseries, if they were to acquire an infection could deteriorate at any time.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. In any event there was something -- well, there was the grunting from baby JE that caused you to instruct Nurse Letby to increase the frequency of the recorded observations and to notify the on-call -- the duty registrar; is that right?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Were those instructions observed?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: I can't remember about the observations, whether they were increased from two to one-hourly, but yes, the registrar did come and review.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Was that done at the first time of asking on your part or not?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: I don't remember.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Now let's move through the shift and let's go to the time of [Baby C]'s collapse, which is recorded on the note -- I shan't take you there -- at about 23.15 hours, so about quarter past 11 on the night of the 13th.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Where were you when you first became aware of a crisis in relation to [Baby C]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: I do not remember where I was, but I was not in nursery 1.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Do you recall what alerted you to the crisis?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: A shout for help.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Do you recall who shouted?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: No.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Do you recall what was shouted?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: I think "help". I don't remember.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. How did you respond?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: I immediately went in.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: On entering nursery 1, what did you see?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: From memory and reading my statement this morning, I saw Mel and Sophie with [Baby C].
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Mel Taylor, Sophie Ellis?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Where were they?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: They were beside his incubator.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And what were they doing?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: They were -- they had a Neopuff device. They were trying to ventilate him because he wasn't breathing.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Do you recall who was doing what?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: No.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. And did you go straight to the incubator?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: I don't remember.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Do you recall whether at that point or soon thereafter you noted his data, as it were, his --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And what did you note?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: I noticed he wasn't breathing and his heart rate was very low.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. Oxygen saturation levels?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Very low.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Did the Neopuffing -- was it successful, did it cause [Baby C] to breathe?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: He didn't begin to breathe, but the Neopuff gave [Baby C] chest movement, so it was -- the Neopuff was breathing for him, but he did not begin to breathe himself.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. Did you notice at this stage anything about his appearance?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: He was -- he didn't look well, he looked very unwell.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: He was mottled.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And was a crash call for the medics put out?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Do you remember who put out the crash call?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: No.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Do you remember who was present when the crash call was put out?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: I remember Lucy being in the nursery at that stage, but I don't remember -- the doctors certainly weren't on the unit.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Okay. For precision, you say being "on the nursery", which nursery?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Sorry, in the neonatal unit. They weren't in the neonatal unit at the time, the doctors. That's why the official crash call had to go out.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. So that's the medics?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Had a doctor been at hand, he or she could have been shouted --

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: One of the tertiary units. And that's the impression you formed; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it remained a constant. And it was a fact of life there that sometimes the ward manager was fighting for more staff to try to stay BAPM compliant?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: The manager will have continually reviewed data on a monthly basis and she will have looked at the amount of admissions versus the BAPM compliance, and if she felt at any point then she would have highlighted that to her seniors.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Didn't you describe it to the police in terms that the ward manager was fighting for more staff, though?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: She will have asked for more staff certainly.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: All right. The word "fighting" comes from you, doesn't it, [Nurse B]?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: I can't remember.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There we are. If you just look down towards the bottom of that page, it's a statement that you will have read, I imagine, recently, [Nurse B]. Can you just see that large paragraph, a few lines up from the bottom?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: (Pause). Yes, that's what I've written.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "I recall that the ward manager was fighting for more staff."

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes?

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes. Mm-hm.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: That's correct. I've quite clearly pointed out that wasn't just a Chester issue.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. And you added this:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "As a staff we worked really hard over that period, missing breaks and doing whatever we could to make it function."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: All right, thank you. We can take that down.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You agree that was not an ideal experience for staff, was it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: No.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And not ideal really for babies, is it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Can you rephrase that differently?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Just because the amount of babies increased doesn't mean we weren't BAPM compliant on every single shift. So for this shift in particular, or any shift that you are making reference to, you will have to look at the care level of the baby versus the BAPM standard, you have to look at that individually.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: The care would have been given because the nurses were missing their breaks.

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.

blocks.text: They indicate what is optimal or best practice, don't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.

blocks.text: Do you agree that it wasn't always the case that you could follow those guidelines on the unit?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: That would... Are you referring to staffing levels or are you referring to, say, the ITU status of the baby an ITU baby being at Chester?

blocks.text: In general, it wasn't always possible to follow the right numbers of staff for the babies who were being looked after, was it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: When... Yes? Are you agreeing with me when I say that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: TPN?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: TPN.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: TPN, yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. I'm not going to go through all of the list but it's carefully set out, isn't it, in the guidelines?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'll add this because we've heard something of these: a baby who has an umbilical venous line is also an intensive care baby; that's correct, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: As a general rule, I'm not going to any particular set, this is just to help us, is the nurse who's looking after a baby meant to put in as much as she or he can remember that is relevant to the period they've looked after the baby?

blocks.text: NURSE B: At an appropriate time, yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: At an appropriate time, yes. I suppose it follows that if a nurse was to make an entry that was put under the wrong set of baby's notes, then a nurse who comes in later won't get to read that entry until that's been corrected?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: It would have been spotted by the nurse caring for the baby where the wrong -- where it was wrong. Does that make sense? And they would have been alerted. But without the notes, everything that has happened -- the notes are your written and you've already had that significant verbal handover at the cot side.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There's that as well.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: So the handover is there as your first -- the notes are there for potential future or further reference.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But a nurse coming on and looking after a baby or other babies, he or she may well go to the written notes just to see the history of the child recently?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Do you agree that, given his size and his prematurity and his conditions, there was a risk that he could die?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: ask you questions about that as well. Your recollection is this may have been at a period when staff were allocated by the shift leader before you came on duty?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So it may well not have been your decision?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: By your recollection, this was a busy shift, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Perhaps something that those people who don't work with babies in units like this may not appreciate, but I'm going to ask you about, is that babies don't necessarily stop in their care requirements at night, do they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: No, it's 24 hours.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It is 24 hours, so shifts can be busy day or night, can't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.

blocks.text: You knew Sophie Ellis because you'd been involved to some extent in her training?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Is that correct? And you were comfortable with her being in the position of being allocated to [Baby C]?

blocks.text: NURSE B: Mm-hm.

blocks.text: Yes. But do you know whether -- I spoke over you, sorry.

blocks.text: NURSE B: It's okay.

blocks.text: NURSE B: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So both [Baby C] and both that baby were intensive care babies?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.

blocks.text: NURSE B: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So because [Baby C]'s CRP was 23, a decision had been taken to do a lumbar puncture, so "AW" is awaiting. And again, that's the test to look for meningitis, to take a sample of fluid, which hadn't been done at that point.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: But somebody had decided, who'd seen him, that he was going to have 7 days of antibiotics either way.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: If we can scroll further down the page, please. M stands for?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Medication.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Could you tell us about the three lines that follow?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So [Baby C] was on some caffeine, which is standard for babies of this gestation. Benpen and gentamicin, so benzylpenicillin and gentamicin are the two standard antibiotics that he would have been given initially if somebody initially had thought about, could this be infection --
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Pausing there, when you tell us about the line above this, someone decided to give him antibiotics for 7 days, they're the two antibiotics --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: -- he'd have been receiving? Okay. And before we move on, the purpose of caffeine?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So some premature babies, they're not designed to be out in the world, they're designed to still be inside mum and sometimes they forget to breathe, and caffeine is a stimulant that helps reduce those apnoeas.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Right, okay. And nystatin?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Nystatin is a preventive medication for oral thrush, that again is common in premature babies.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Thank you. I'm not sure -- what's in the --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The next circle says "met" for metabolic. And this is the comment that he was jaundiced and it looks like his phototherapy, so his blue light treatment for the jaundice, had been stopped at 7 pm.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: So pausing there, jaundice very briefly is?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So jaundice is very common in newborn babies. It's a result of their blood cells not living as long as adult blood cells do and liver immaturity is more common in premature babies, so when they break down their red blood cells they make something called bilirubin, which makes them yellow. If that's left untreated it can cause damage to their brains but we treat at a very low level to prevent that.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: And the answer may well be in the line, but how is it treated?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The phototherapy is a blue light.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: I've asked you to slow down. You naturally speak very quickly and you're using some quite complicated words. It is not me trying to take a note, it's someone who is a professional stenographer who is struggling to keep pace.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It's been a problem before. I apologise.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Jaundice, you have told us, is a condition whereby the red blood cells don't break down properly and cause a yellow colouration to the skin?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: The red blood cells in newborn babies break down quicker than they do in adults and then what happens to that breakdown product is that it is converted by the liver and then it's excreted, but several steps along that process aren't as
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: efficient in premature babies, which is where their jaundice comes from.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: And the appearance is?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Babies often look yellow.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: And again the treatments used for jaundice?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is ultraviolet light. They have a light put above their incubator or cot on exposed skin, which helps convert the bilirubin into a form that they can excrete.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Right, thank you. I think you told us that the time, 19.00, suggest that that treatment had come to an end (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That had stopped but it's something that we would check again. It looks like the plan was to check it again at 2 in the morning.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Thank you. Is that:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "OE: handles well"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On examination, handles well."
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: "HS"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: His heart sounds are normal. He didn't have any murmurs to be heard. He was well perfused, so that means kind of he was warm, he was nice and pink. Capillary refill time is another measure of perfusion and that was less than 2 seconds, which is normal.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Okay, let's pause there. So capillary refill time, I think we've heard, is the test where a clinician presses their finger on the baby's skin?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: And then times how long before the colour returns?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: We've then got a small diagram. Tell us what that is.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think we've been told before. Is that the lungs?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: They're a pair of lungs. I have written "good AE", which is good air entry.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: And we can see the word "active" to the right-hand side?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Active in what way?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This suggests that in terms of "handles well" -- and "active" suggests that this was a baby who was --
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: (overspeaking) so he would be active and moving round.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: The next diagram, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is an abdomen. I've commented that his abdomen was soft, he had bowel sounds, and there was no discolouration on his abdomen.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: We've heard that earlier that day, round about lunchtime, there was an X-ray which showed a lot of air in [Baby C]'s tummy. Is that examination relevant to that in any way?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So with a -- lots of air, presumably a distended tummy, the two thought processes being "infection-related something", but he is also on CPAP, so lots of babies on CPAP do have distended gassy tummies. I haven't commented on distension so I can't tell you whether his tummy was distended or not, but there's nothing worrying about his tummy in what I've documented.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: At that particular time --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, at that point.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: All right. Then we touched on the plan. Just take us through the plan, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So "a gas" refers to a blood gas, which is a blood test we do to look at parameters around ventilation. "Bili"
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: is bilirubin, which would be to look at his jaundice level to see which way that had gone after we'd stopped treatment. And then glucose -- I presume at some point there had been either some concern about his sugars or we'd changed something with his fluids that meant that we wanted to look at what his blood sugar was. And "chase" implies that somebody prior to this has done a
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: full blood count, the results of which are not back, so an acknowledgement that we need to look at that.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: All right. You signed off on the right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: That was -- did you say that was a routine review of [Baby C]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This looks like a routine review of a baby who would have technically been an intensive care baby, so just a routine nightly review. This doesn't imply that there were concerns about him.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Okay. Did you carry out a routine review the following night, on 13 June?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: From my recollection, he had a cardiac arrest prior to me seeing him.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: So you were planning to do so?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: But there was then an incident before you had the opportunity to do so?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: I'm going to ask you about that. Do you recall roughly what time that incident took place?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think it was pre-midnight.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Okay. Shall we go, in fact, to the tile so you can look at your notes again. I'll just check the number. It's 187, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: That might be a good point, in fact, my Lord, to take a break. I'd forgotten the time.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's all right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We'll break off. Could you be ready, please, to continue at 2.05? Just about an hour, give or take a minute. Remember your obligations and responsibilities. No conversations and no research.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much. 2.05.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Davis, can you be back ready to start again at 2.05, please? Thank you very much. And don't talk to anyone about the case.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the absence of the jury)
I should say, my Lord, I realise it was I who read out the name when going through the statement.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Don't worry. It was inadvertent.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I apologise for that. I'd programmed myself to use initials elsewhere but not when I was reading from the statement.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Don't worry. The representative in court certainly was alive to it, I'm sure he will have -- he wouldn't...
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm grateful, my Lord, thank you. I apologise.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Right, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The short adjournment)
(In the presence of the jury)

Dr Davis, you were about to go on and tell us something of [Baby C]'s collapse on the night shift of the 13th into 14 June. Before we go on to that, could you just tell us, please, how you were alerted to what was taking place?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I believe I had a crash bleep.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Tell us then, please, what you did when you got that crash bleep?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So the crash bleep would have said to go urgently to the neonatal unit, which is what I would have done. I think from memory I was relatively close when it happened.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Tell us, please, at this stage from your memory, what you remember when you arrived.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I remember arriving on the neonatal unit with a lot of activity around [Baby C]. There was a Guedel airway in situ --
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Let's pause there. So where was [Baby C] when you went into --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: [Baby C] was in room 1 on the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Okay. And when you describe activity, that was around his incubator, presumably?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So there were several nurses there at the time.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Right. Can you remember who?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not for certain. I remember there being a senior nurse, who I think was [Nurse B], who was clearly in charge and directing what was going on, but beyond that, I don't remember who was there.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Okay. I'd like to take you then, please, to your note rather than rely on your memory. If we can go, please, into that tile we had up. 187.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we can look at the note behind it, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: A little bit out of time order. If we can scroll down, please. I'm sure you recognise that's your handwriting from earlier?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: It's a note from you, 14 June, timed at 1.30, and as the heading says, written in retrospect. We can see:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "23.26, crash bleeped to attend NICU."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Neonatal intensive care unit.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: "Myself and SHO Jian Min Hor arrived on unit in less than 1 minute."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That was your recollection a moment or two ago, you were very quick?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Then you've noted:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On arrival, Guedel airway in situ."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We've heard a couple of times about a Guedel airway, a device that is used to assist in opening the airway, we understand?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Do you remember who was using that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't know who put it in, it was already in when I got there.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: "Being bagged by Neopuff [or via Neopuff] by nursing staff."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I've already asked you if you can remember and the only person you remember is [Nurse B]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: And:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Chest compressions in progress."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I take it you can't remember who was administering them? Okay. Your note says:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Occasional intermittent gasps noted."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Tell us, please, how [Baby C] appeared when you arrived at the NICU?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I think from --
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Can you remember what he looked like when you arrived?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, other than I think somewhere in my statement I put that he looked pale.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Obviously, intermittent gasps, you're talking about [Baby C] there when you assessed him. Just moving to the second line, please:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Chest compressions stopped."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: At what stage did that take place?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: As a registrar on arrival, my first job would have been to assess him from the beginning to see what was happening. He obviously had a monitor on, which was showing a heart rate. But while chest compressions are ongoing it's difficult to know if that's his heart rate or if that's a response to the chest compressions. So the implication of chest compressions stopped is that I would have asked them to be stopped briefly for me to assess [Baby C], so for me to listen to see if he had a heart rate and to see if he was breathing himself.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Okay. Does your note assist whether -- when those chest compressions were stopped (inaudible)?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "No HR/RR" is no heart rate or respiratory rate on auscultation.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Auscultation is the use of a stethoscope?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: How did that combination strike you at that point?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So it was very unusual for that to be the case. So I've been to a number of collapses of neonates over my career and usually, even with the very smallest, sickest babies, there is some heart rate, but it's a slow heart rate, or there is some respiratory effort, but there was nothing in [Baby C]'s case at all.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: So neither of those features -- just simply absent on both counts?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So he wasn't breathing, he was gasping intermittently, but there was certainly no -- I remember clearly that there was no heart rate at all.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Okay. So what did you decide to do?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's clear from this situation that [Baby C] needed significant resuscitation. So at this point, we've restarted the chest compressions by whoever was doing them and I've asked for someone to go and call Dr Gibbs, who was the consultant on call, who would have been at home and not on site. And I have taken over managing [Baby C]'s airway, so I've taken the Neopuff off whoever was doing that.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Let's pause there: is that your responsibility as the doctor to take over the airway?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's not set in stone, it's usually what you go to as the most experienced person. I would have been the only person who could intubate, so there's always the question is that what needs doing.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: All right. So you took over the airway. Did you attempt to intubate?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I think I did.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Was that successful?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, it wasn't. So I think -- I can just about see on the bottom line there -- when I've gone to look, I've seen where the tube needed to go, but his vocal cords were very swollen so I have not been able to -- so I will have abandoned that attempt and then what I've done is I've got a smaller tube, because if you're having difficulty often if you go to a smaller tube and you're using something called an introducer, that makes the tube a bit stiffer.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Let's just pause there for a minute. So you went to intubate?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: And tell us what you saw, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I got a good view of where I should be able to -- where the tube needed to go. But the hole that was there wasn't visible because his vocal cords were swollen.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: You have used another term there on your note, "Swollen and"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Oedematous.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: What does that mean, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Kind of fluid swollen.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Did you notice that when you first went to intubate [Baby C] or was that something that developed?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, so that was my first attempt, so before I'd even attempted to put anything in.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: So you attempted -- we have heard that the numbers 3 and 2.5 refer to the size of the tube that you are attempting to -- with which you are attempting to intubate. So it was a size 3 that you were unable to introduce and you went on to tell us what you were doing with the 2.5.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I've made the decision to try again with a smaller tube and something called an introducer. So an introducer is a bit of wire that's plastic covered, that you put inside the tube that makes it a little bit stiffer. So if you've got either a very small hole or you're trying to go through something that's quite difficult, it just gives you a little more -- the tube is less likely to just bend and...
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Were you successful with the introducer?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No. I have had two further attempts at doing that and again have not been able to intubate. So at that point I have taken the decision not to --
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Okay --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- attempt further.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Your note says:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Unable to pass ET tube as cords..."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that plus plus?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: What does the plus plus --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I presume the word "swollen" should be there.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Okay. Then the next line, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Clear oral secretions and no blood seen."
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Right. So we know that the Guedel airway is in place and as your next note suggests, Neopuffing continued using that particular device?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So it would have had to have been removed in order for me to attempt intubation but then by re-putting it in and using the Neopuff, we were getting good chest movement so it was achieving what we needed to. So that's why we didn't have -- I didn't have further attempts at intubation at that point because we were managing the airway in a different way.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: "Chest compressions continued."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Any success with the resuscitation that you were attempting?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: We've heard that there is a list of medication that's given, adrenaline and bicarb being two of those, bicarbonate of soda being two of those measures.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Next line, please:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Heart rate checked?"
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Heart rate checked approximately every 30 seconds..."
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Which would be standard for newborn resuscitation:
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: "... to reassess."
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: And throughout we didn't hear any heart rate at all.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: So no response to any of the resuscitation attempts --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: -- that you undertook?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: None at all.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Okay. The next note, I suspect, speaks for itself.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Dr Gibbs arrived as the second dose of bicarbonate of soda was given and you have put:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "See previous notes for full resus details."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's what we have just been through?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I presume that is Dr Gibbs' notes that you showed me briefly above mine.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Right, okay, we will leave those for Dr Gibbs if we may.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: There's a list underneath of drugs given. I am not proposing to go through each and every one of them but is it your recollection that that's an accurate record of each and every attempt to administer drugs to resuscitate [Baby C]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The likelihood is in a situation like this the SHO who was present, who I believe was a GP trainee rather than a paediatric trainee, so had limited neonatal experience, would have made notes as we went along as to what was given and then I've written the times down subsequently from that contemporaneous note.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: And I think we may -- if we go down to the next line, please, that may explain:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Above prescribed on printed drug chart retrospectively."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Okay. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Your next note is at 2 am. Did [Baby C] respond to resuscitation once Dr Gibbs had arrived?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No. So from memory, we had a fairly prolonged attempt at actively resuscitating [Baby C] with multiple drugs.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: His parents were called. Mum was still an inpatient at the time and I believe dad was called in from home.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It became obvious that we really were not winning, but we hadn't got a heart rate, so a discussion would have been had with the parents as to where we were and a decision taken to stop resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: That failure to respond to resuscitation, how did that strike you at the time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's really unusual. So even the smallest, sickest babies will usually respond in some way, even if only for a brief period of time, that we would get a heart rate or we'd get them back for a short period and they may go on to have subsequent arrests if they're really unwell. But this was clearly very unusual at the time that we had absolutely no response in a baby who had been relatively stable.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Right, okay. So not responding to resuscitation. We've heard there comes a point where a decision is discussed amongst the medical staff; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: And do you remember that discussion taking place in this case?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't remember what was actually said, but I remember that a decision was taken that active resuscitation was seemingly futile, that we needed to stop.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: And were the parents engaged in that conversation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The parents would have been told that that's what we were thinking.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Okay. Now, did those attempts at resuscitation, once a decision had been reached, stop immediately?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, they didn't. We asked the parents, as would be standard practice, if they had any spiritual or religious needs
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: or wants for [Baby C], and christening/baptism was discussed with them. That was something that they said they would like. In order for babies to be christened or baptised, that takes place while the baby is technically and legally still alive.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: So for that reason, although we stopped giving further drugs and I believe we turned the monitors off, we continued the chest compressions and the bagging while we were waiting for that process to happen.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Okay. I think, perhaps for reasons we needn't go into, it took a while for the baptism to be completed.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It didn't feel like it at the time, but I've aware from looking at the times that, yes (overspeaking).
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Yes, all right. And once baptism had been completed, what happened then?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Towards the end of -- during the baptism, we had something called a capnograph on the end of the tube -- because [Baby C] was intubated by this point.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Pausing there, capnograph?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: A capnograph is a plastic device that sits on the end of the tube and it measures -- it changes colour if carbon dioxide is coming up the tube.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Because the principle being that being oxygen breathed in with carbon dioxide but more carbon dioxide breathed out?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Overspeaking) and it's a way you can tell in babies who are breathing, it's an indication that that tube is in the right place.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: But babies in cardiac arrest, such as [Baby C], we wouldn't expect that colour change to be happening.
