Again, I'm anxious to make it plain when I ask questions about this I appreciate I am standing here in the relative calm of a courtroom and when you're dealing with things as they unfold in real life it can be more intense sometimes and more difficult than when we stand here reflecting on it now.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I recognise that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's crucial, if there's a collapse, to maintain breathing -there are a number of things that are crucial but breathing is key, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: The jury have heard you and others talk about efforts to intubate or to keep breathing rates at a particular level, saturations at a particular level, and that's because respiration has got to take place if anything else is going to work and if it's going to be successful?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: The collapse, we understand from Nurse Ellis' note, is at about 23.15. About that time. The steps that the nurses can take to support breathing are limited after a certain point, aren't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Depending on the experience of the nurses present, yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: So for example, to intubate so that a baby can be put on a ventilator, is certainly something in this situation that a doctor would have to do?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: A doctor or an advanced practitioner, yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: None of the nurses looking after [Baby C] on this particular night were advanced practitioner nurses?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: None of them were able to intubate, no.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: In a tertiary unit, like Arrowe Park or Liverpool Women's Hospital, would you expect to have advanced practitioner nurses or a higher number of advanced practitioner nurses?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: On a night shift or at any point?
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: On a night shift then.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So relatively the tertiary units you mentioned are bigger units so, yes, they have more staff.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Again, this isn't said critically of staff at the Countess of Chester in this way, but are the nursing staff at a place like Arrowe Park then, some of them, more able or able to intubate in a way that they couldn't do with [Baby C] on this night at the Countess of Chester?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: As far as I'm aware nursing staff do not intubate.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: So they never intubate?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The advanced nurse practitioners do, but nursing staff don't.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Then I wasn't clear about that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Are there advanced nurse practitioners at Arrowe Park who could intubate that weren't present at the Countess of Chester?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I can't comment about Arrowe because I have never worked at Arrowe but certainly in Liverpool Women's Hospital, when I
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: worked there in the 6 months prior to this job, yes, there were, but didn't do night shifts.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Okay. In terms of consultant cover can you help us with this? Was it Liverpool Women's Hospital you worked at?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Was there a greater level of on-site consultant cover in the neonatal units there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Certainly not. Overnight they were on call from home.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: On call from home. What about in the day?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In the day there was two consultants on but that was one for intensive care and one for high dependency, which was relative to the number of babies they had.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Yes, because, of course, they have babies with a higher acuity there, don't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: At Liverpool Women's Hospital, during the day, there would be two consultants on the neonatal unit?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The two consultants responsible for, not necessarily on the unit.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Responsible for, yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Which is a higher level than you'd have had during the day at the Countess of Chester, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In terms of there was one consultant covering the ward and the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: That's right. Covering the children's ward and the neonatal unit?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Two for the neonatal unit at the Liverpool Women's Hospital?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, but it's four or five times the size.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Yes. Are you aware if there's ever an issue in placing the right baby in the right hospital for the level of care that he or she needs?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: What do you mean by issue?
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Well, does a baby that needs to get to a tertiary unit always get to a tertiary unit on the basis of care alone or are there other considerations?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: They're always discussed with the tertiary unit and a decision about where to place them will often be guided by them. Some babies -- for example, usually there's a cut-off with ventilated babies, that we would discuss them at a set period of time, be that 24 or 48 hours with the network saying, ideally these babies should be in a tertiary unit --
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Slow down a little bit, Dr Davis.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: So there would be a discussion?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There'd be a discussion and it's a risk-benefit discussion because moving a baby is inherently dangerous.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Pause there a moment, please. Before that you said something about the baby being in the right unit. What were you going to say about that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So if a baby is intubated in a district general hospital, such as Chester, there would be a discussion at a certain point with the tertiary unit. Part of that discussion would be should we keep them or should they go elsewhere. Whilst there is -- my understanding is at the time there's some evidence around 48 hours kind of being the cut-off for district general hospitals. If that baby's expected to come off a ventilator in the short term keeping them is a lot less risky than putting them in an ambulance. So it's a discussion, there's no black and white in these discussions.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: And did something as simple, that may be fundamental, as bed availability ever play a part in deciding which baby went to which unit?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, because we could always transfer out of region if needed.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Although, as you say, the fact of transport can be an added risk to a baby, can't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Any transport is a risk, yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Right. Getting back to what I was asking you, and that was my fault for taking you away from that, there are some questions I wanted to ask you. The nurses who were looking after [Baby C] after his collapse had got to the point of inserting a Guedel airway; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: And is that a preliminary to intubation taking place?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, it's an alternative method of maintaining an airway.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: When you arrived -- you got to the unit just looking at your note -- you can scroll back if you want, but you got back there at about 23.26. Perhaps we could just go back, Mr Murphy, a page. Sorry, go forwards a page to Dr Davis' note.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We can see here, it might be approximate, but 23.26 is when you received the bleep?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I imagine that's the time of bleep.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: You were on the children's ward at that point?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: But you got across to the neonatal unit within a minute?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: When you arrived there, the Guedel airway was in place we can see and the nursing staff were -- is that using the Neopuff on [Baby C]?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: And chest compressions were in progress. Can it be said at that point whether he was receiving the oxygen that he needed or was he not in all probability?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So I presume I -- although I haven't documented it, it would be our standard practice in this situation to be using 100% oxygen, so they were doing all they could.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: I haven't commented on his chest movements at this point.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Why did you take the decision that it was necessary to intubate?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's a good question and something that maybe reflects on the decision-making at the time. I don't think intubating or
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: not intubating was a right or wrong answer. The advantages of intubation -- if you can intubate a baby and secure the tube, it frees somebody up, it frees -- you need to be less skilled to bag via a secured tube than a non-secured tube but it doesn't -as long as you're getting chest movement, ET tube versus a Guedel airway doesn't make any difference to what you're achieving.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Thank you for explaining that. Is there any issue of him not receiving the oxygen that he would have needed via the Neopuff but he would have received it if he was on the ventilator and intubated?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So in this situation he wouldn't have gone on to a ventilator; he would have been Neopuffed via the tube.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Right. When you came to intubate you say that you became aware that the cords were swollen and blocking the route.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: By the time you saw those cords, he'd already had a Guedel airway inserted by the nursing staff, hadn't he?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Was that removed for when you came to do the intubation, Dr Davis?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it has to be.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: So as to how they came to be swollen, that's difficult for you to say from what you're describing?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: A Guedel airway should sit much higher than the cords.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Right, okay. Or as to when they became swollen is something you can't tell us?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I can't say that, no.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: You weren't able to intubate; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Would he have been receiving the oxygen that he needed over the period that you were attempting to intubate him?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So you stop bagging for a brief period of time, but part of the reason we abandon an attempt -- so it looked -- I... I will have had an attempt and then stopped to re-bag. We don't
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: want to leave him for prolonged periods of time without bagging. So in that moment, yes, but we usually put a limit of about 30 seconds in which you'll try and then, if you're not successful, you abandon it and carry on with what you were doing, which is why after these three attempts I didn't try any further.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Right. Dr Gibbs, I think from the note, arrived at about 11.35 pm.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Can I just ask about that. Was the decision to call Dr Gibbs taken as soon as the collapse happened or at a later stage?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: From my notes it looks like I've arrived and I have asked someone to call. So certainly in that situation, with a child in cardiac arrest, I would have asked for the consultant to be called straightaway.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: And then he arrives at about 11.35, which is about 20 minutes after the collapse?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, which is obviously very -- is very quick for a consultant from home.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Yes, although any period of time without receiving oxygen properly is potentially damaging, isn't it, for a baby -- or anyone?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, but he was receiving resuscitation prior to the consultant's arrival.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Could I just ask you to confirm something about [Baby C]'s breathing during all of this. Again, I appreciate we're talking about a little person when I'm saying this, I'm not trying to sound too academic about it, but I need to ask you these questions.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You've described, when you were telling the police about this that -- this is at some point during the intubation process, after you have seen his cords:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "[You] could see however that [Baby C]'s chest was moving and his saturations levels were good with the ventilatory support we were providing. Therefore our resuscitation efforts were working correctly."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So we can understand, does that mean he was effectively at that point getting the oxygen that he needed?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So he -- we were moving his chest, which means we were moving air in and out of his lungs. And I believe that (inaudible) saturation monitor, he would have had a monitor on, which would have had a reading, which would have measured the oxygenation in the blood that we were pumping around via chest compressions. But that -- but a measure of oxygenation in presumably a hand or a foot isn't the same as what we were perfusing elsewhere. We don't measure his brain perfusion, we don't measure his blood pressure and things like that, we just measured his peripheral oxygen saturations, which were showing up as reasonable.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: And so is that with why you say there were questions raised as to whether or not he would have received sufficient oxygen to be well enough to preserve life beyond when you did?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In terms of why we didn't restart intensive care?
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Yes, yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: [Baby C] had had a huge period of time without a heart rate and although we were moving his chest and we were putting oxygen in and out of his lungs, we know from experience and from -- we know what happens to other children that we've seen, the effect of even brief periods of time of cardiac arrest and [Baby C]'s period of time in cardiac arrest was really long.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Can I just ask this (inaudible) I need to ask you, Dr Davis: did the delay in being able to intubate him in your opinion create any issue that made it more difficult for [Baby C] to be resuscitated?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No. And as a more experienced doctor now, I would be even less likely to have even tried because we were moving his chest, which is the important thing.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Yes. All right. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Re-examination by MR ASTBURY
Just a couple of questions from me. You told my learned friend that it was not normal to see dark bile but common in premature babies or not uncommon.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: When you see bile like that and taking into account the constellation of other features in this case and all the other information to hand, would you expect a collapse as sudden and as like this in such circumstances?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Absolutely not. I've seen a lot of babies with significant abdominal issues and even as far as babies who have necrotising enterocolitis that have perforated their bowel, so made a hole in their bowel, so the air's come out and into their abdomen, they don't behave and they don't die in the way that [Baby C] died.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Okay. In the context of swelling to the vocal cords that you saw, you were asked about the Guedel airway and you said it sits above the cords. Could you just explain that to us, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So a Guedel airway -- so the vocal cords are where you'd put the tubes through. I don't know whether you've seen pictures of them but they are a bit -- there are kind of two bits that sit and open and close as you breathe.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: And when you intubate, you would go through the hole that's there.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: A Guedel airway is not an invasive secure airway that goes through the cords, it just -- they're much shorter. Obviously, I don't know, I can't recall what size was put in or how it would be put in, but I wouldn't expect a Guedel airway to have caused that swelling.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Where would it sit? Where would the Guedel airway sit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It sits above the cords to hold the airway open.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Right, okay. I have no more questions. Does my Lord have any questions?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't, thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That's it?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, we don't expect this witness, at the moment, to be required.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's not anticipated that you will be required to give evidence again during the course of this trial, but certainly you have now completed your evidence in relation to this baby. Although you have finished your evidence and you're unlikely to be giving evidence again, would you please not talk to anyone about your evidence or anything to do with this case until the trial is all over?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Thank you very much. You'll understand why that is.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Particularly if it's someone who's going to be a witness in the case and talking about it is not appropriate. It's said to every witness who's given evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIS

blocks.text: Or until the trial is over. Thank you very much indeed.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That's a good moment to have a break. We'll have our midafternoon break now and then...
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY
