Examination-in-chief by MR ASTBURY
Could we begin with your full name, please?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: John Michael Gibbs.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Your profession, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm a retired consultant paediatrician. I used to work at the Countess of Chester Hospital.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you in a moment specifically about events in June 2015 when I understand you were employed there in that capacity, but could I first ask, please, when you first qualified at a doctor?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you. You hold a number of qualifications.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Can you summarise them for us, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Oh. My basic medical degree was bachelor of medicine, bachelor of surgery and I also have BSc in biochemistry.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Member of the Royal College of Physicians, fellow of the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, a medical doctorate and diploma in child health.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. When did you become a consultant paediatrician?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you. When did you start work at the Countess of Chester?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Did you have an educational role at the hospital?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What was that, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All of us consultants were educational supervisors for several junior doctors in our department.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And did you at the time have a particular interest in any specialty?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was a general paediatrician with an interest in neonatology, as we all were for the nature of the job in Chester, in that district general hospital, but my particular interests were child development, disability and epilepsy.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. I have already indicated I'm going to ask you questions about events in June 2015. I'm particularly interested, please, in a baby called [Baby C]. We've heard quite a bit about [Baby C]'s birth and condition at birth and the first 2 days of his life. I'm going to concentrate, please, on the contact you had with [Baby C] directly.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: On 13 June in particular, am I right, that you were actually on duty within the unit that particular day?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Obviously these events took place 7 years ago.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I prepared a statement two and a half years after [Baby C]'s birth and death and I hadn't seen his notes since then and I'm now retired, so I can't remember all the details of what went on, but I'm quite happy to be shown any records that are relevant and I can confirm them.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: From my statement, I'd seen [Baby C] several times during the first few days of his life. I had seen him on the morning of 13 June. The registrar, Dr Ogden, had done a ward round, but I'd come round to see some of the babies on the unit that morning and there's an entry in the medical notes from Dr Ogden saying I had reviewed [Baby C] that morning and a suggestion of what future treatment plans we might offer him.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: In fairness to you I think we should go to the notes if that's what you're relying on, please. There's a screen to the right. If we can start at slide 77, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we can click into that. Dr Gibbs, you will see, first of all, a summary on the first page of the notes that lie behind this document. But if we can click into the notes themselves, we can see there initially a note by Dr Ogden timed at 9.30 that particular morning, 13 June.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we scroll down. And down again, please. We can see at the bottom -- I don't think it's your handwriting, but there's an indication, "Reviewed by Dr Gibbs". Can you see that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I think it's Dr Ogden again from the signature at the bottom of that that put that entry in, saying that I'd reviewed [Baby C].
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. Does that help jog your memory in that limited regard?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Um... There was no particular concern about [Baby C] that morning. He did have some gastric aspirates and we knew that being a baby who was premature, but also small even for being premature, because of reduced blood flow to him from the placenta inside the womb before he was born, that he was at risk of complications, one of them being this condition known as necrotising enterocolitis.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Now, the gastric aspirates he was showing were not of any concern at that time, they weren't copious --
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I'm going to ask you to pause there. Only because what you're saying is being noted down elsewhere. It's all very helpful but we need to make sure that particular person keeps up.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You were telling us about the risk of NEC and what had actually been seen by way of -- was it aspirates in that particular regard?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, aspirates but looking back --
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Would it help you to see the full note of Dr Ogden?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, no, I'm fine, I'm just looking up at the notes we've got on the screen here. When Dr Ogden's written OE, on examination, about the eighth line down, it says:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Abdo soft not distended."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Which is very reassuring because when babies are developing necrotising enterocolitis, their abdomens become distended, so it was good to note that his abdomen was soft.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Dr Ogden doesn't record everything that I felt when I reviewed him, but the fact she doesn't record anything else means I would have agreed with the findings that she has put down. So his tummy is nice and soft, but he was having some gastric aspirates, and that can sometimes be common in any baby that has not been fed as the stomach naturally produces some acid and stomach secretions --
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Pause there, then, please, sorry. We know that, at this stage, [Baby C] hasn't had any feed by mouth.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So that's a consideration when it comes to these sort of aspirates from the stomach?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. I'm not... Well, yes in that if a baby is being fed, that helps the stomach to empty and to get the gastric juices and all the other intestinal juices flowing. And until that baby starts feeding and having milk into its stomach, sometimes the gastric acid can accumulate in the stomach.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right. And would that be, as far as you're concerned, consistent with what was being found by way of aspirates up to that stage?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, yes, but those aspirates can irritate the stomach, as can the nasogastric tube, the plastic tube lying in the
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: stomach. And that's why I had recommended starting some ranitidine, which is what Dr Ogden is writing at the bottom of that page, "IV ranitidine". That's an antacid, to counter the acid in the stomach.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That's the reason for the medication?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The next line:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Hold off feeds..."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. The aspirates that [Baby C] was producing at that time, which I think were around about up to 2ml each time the nurses checked, were not of concern but if the aspirates got steadily larger then that could indicate his bowel wasn't functioning normally. And if he started vomiting that would be a concern because that can be a sign of early necrotising enterocolitis.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And necrotising enterocolitis is felt to be precipitated by starting feeds, if a baby's prone to necrotising enterocolitis, which is why at this stage the plan was just to monitor the amount of aspirates and to hold off giving any feeds at the moment.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. And I think the note made on your behalf reads -is that "Review this PM"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "If aspirates not getting worse start trophic feeds"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that means start a small amount of feed, a trophic feed. It's not going to be full nutrition, which [Baby C] was receiving at that stage, that's just a small amount of feeds, and that would allow the stomach to empty better.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Your note continues:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "If worsens, repeat AXR."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's abdominal X-ray. If the aspirates got larger or he started vomiting, it doesn't mean he is developing necrotising enterocolitis, but that would be a concern.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: One way of helping to diagnose early NEC is by taking an abdominal X-ray, but also if there is a suspicion a child may be developing NEC, they shouldn't be fed into the stomach because that can worsen the NEC and that's why it says if the aspirates
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: are worsening to do an X-ray. And to change antibiotics is because [Baby C] was already on antibiotics from birth or from early soon after birth. If you suspect a baby may be suffering from NEC, then there's a different range of antibiotics that are given particularly to cover bowel bacteria.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That was the plan if it got worse.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think you had some more contact with [Baby C] later that day, if we can go, please, to slide 108, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: At the top of the notes there we can see -- I think this time it is your handwriting.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It is, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And we can see an entry timed at 15.55 that afternoon.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Can you explain to us, please, what you recall of that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That is "US head", which is abbreviation of ultrasound of the head, but really it's of [Baby C]'s brain and it says normal because I had performed an ultrasound of his head.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Premature babies are at risk of having bleeds in the central parts of their brain and so we do intermittently ultrasound scan babies born at about 34 weeks to check whether there are any bleeds in their head. That scan was normal in [Baby C].
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I don't say much else apart from just signing it there but if I'd been worried about [Baby C] in any other way at the time I did his head scan I would normally note that in the notes. So the fact I noted nothing else means there was nothing else that was concerning me about [Baby C] at that time.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Nothing else about the scan or [Baby C] generally?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: [Baby C] generally because I have to examine him to scan him, and if I'd been concerned about him at that stage I ought to have reported something else in the notes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Pausing there, you'd have actually been present for the scan taking place?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I did the scan.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. And that would have, in any event, resulted in an examination of [Baby C] at or around 15.55 that afternoon?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not necessarily a full examination of the nature of the examination recorded earlier in the day by Dr Ogden, but I have to look at the baby and scan his head, but little babies aren't all dressed up at that stage, so if I'd been concerned about him in any way or the nurses had been concerned about him, or his observations had been significantly abnormal, I would have written something else other than just ultrasound of his head.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. We're going to come to what else you wrote about [Baby C] in a minute but that I think, according to the notes, was your last contact with [Baby C] during the day shift.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I think that particular night you were paediatric cover on-call consultant?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is it right later that night you received an emergency call?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I did. Can I talk about the notes here or just...?
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I think we should go through the notes. I'm going to ask you to break it up a little bit for that reason that notes are being taken but given what you said at the outset and the fact that you have relied on your notes, I think that's probably, if I may say so, the best way to do it.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If you can take us through your note line by line and explain where necessary and I'll hopefully prompt what it is that you have noted.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: As is often the case when dealing with an emergency, it's not possible to deal with the emergency appropriately and write in the notes at the same time, so the note entries are after the event. So this note entry is made at 00.30 on the 14th but referring back to events that had happened over an hour or so before that.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And I have received -- I was on call from home in the evening and I was on call for the whole night.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I was called at around 11.28. It's sometimes a bit difficult when you're phoned at night to know exactly what the time is the
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: moment the phone call starts, but around 11.28, and asked to attend urgently.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I can't remember who spoke to me. It's often the hospital switchboard rather than anyone on the neonatal unit or wherever I've been asked to attend. I was told there's an emergency, I can't remember the details, but often it was said there is an arrest, which just means a patient in dire straits, who's often stopped breathing or their heart rate has stopped or heart has stopped.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And it was on the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I arrived there at about 25 to 12, 11.35.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Pause there for a moment, let everybody catch up. What is it that you found when you arrived, doctor?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, little [Baby C] was being ventilated with a Neopuff ventilation. Has Neopuff been explained? Do the jury know about Neopuff?
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes, thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So Neopuff ventilation was in progress and cardiac compressions were in progress. So [Baby C]'s chest was being compressed to help his circulation, to empty blood out of his heart.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: [Baby C] had a poor colour and I have noted he was pale and mottled.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't talk about the actual colour and I can't remember exactly. It will be a purply/blue-y mottled colour, which is not uncommon in someone in a cardiac arrest situation because there's very little -- no circulation.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. I think it says "no heart sounds"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. I couldn't -- because I'm writing this, this is what I would have observed. There's no heart sounds.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We feel for pulses and in babies a good place to feel for the pulse is in the groin, that's the femoral pulse, when the chest compressions are stopped. Because the whole idea of pressing the chest is to squash the heart and squeeze some blood out of it and you can feel weak pulses when you're doing that.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But to assess a child during resuscitation you stop for about 10 seconds to check whether there's any heart sounds, to check whether there's any pulse, and to check whether the child makes any breathing efforts. But there was no respiratory effort when the ventilation was stopped.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So there were no signs of life, essentially, in [Baby C]. But resuscitation to provide him with some circulation and to ventilate for him was being done.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right. On the subject of ventilation I think the next line suggests -- is it intubated or intubation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Intubated and that's a -- size 2.5 ETT, so that's just naming the size, a small diameter tube called the endotracheal tube, which is passed through the mouth down into the windpipe, the trachea, through which you can provide much more effective ventilation than just using a Neopuff mask.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right. In brackets?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That says "with introducer". Now, I don't specify here all the details. I don't usually use an introducer immediately; that's when it's difficult to intubate.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I think there must have been attempts beforehand to intubate that were unsuccessful and the introducer just stiffens the tube and assists intubation, that's putting the tube down into the trachea.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: All right. You can't assist with what those difficulties may or may not have been?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You don't remember now?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, and I wasn't there at the time because I've just arrived. Well, I'd arrived after those attempts, I think, because I can't remember it in detail, who was doing what at the time 7 years ago or 2 years later when I did my statement.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Hence we'll continue with the notes if that's more helpful.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Good chest movement"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's having intubated, getting the tube down into the trachea, there is good chest movement, and you could hear air. So that's the air entry. R and L is right and left so you could hear entry on both sides.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: It's important to say R and L because sometimes the tube's not gone into the right place, it might have gone down one lung and not ventilating both lungs, but those observations show that ventilation was effective at that time.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So shows that air is going in and out of lungs. Is the baby breathing or is that simply the ventilation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's someone ventilating [Baby C] through the endotracheal tube.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right. I'm sorry, I can't read the next line. I can see it ends "ETT".
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Continued vent [which is ventilation] via endotracheal tube."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So continued with the ventilation down the tube.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Having established it was in the right place and effectively ventilating both lungs, continued the ventilation through that tube.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And cardiac compressions. It really means continued cardiac compressions as well.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I should just add, although I say you get more effective ventilate by putting the endotracheal tube down into the windpipe, you can get good ventilation from the Neopuff as well, but it's just more effective and more secure, and you get less air blown into the stomach if you've got the tube right down into the windpipe rather than blowing it into the mouth with a Neopuff.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Next line:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Repeated adrenaline via long line."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I think if we scroll a bit further down --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And we gave [Baby C] quite a lot of adrenaline. That's six doses there he was given throughout --
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Relatively speaking is that a lot of adrenaline in any given resuscitation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. You give adrenaline usually every 4 minutes or so.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: It is hard to time it exactly every 3 or 4 minutes. It just indicates it was quite a prolonged resuscitation effort in progress to have given 6 doses of adrenaline.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes. We can also see on your note, three boluses of saline?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Two boluses of -- I can't see that, sorry.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's 4.2%. That's just the chemical symbol for sodium bicarbonate. So that's -- the saline, the boluses are 10ml each and [Baby C] is a little baby so each of those 10ml should help to restore circulation to ensure's got a good volume in his cardiovascular system.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And then when there's been prolonged poor circulation the body becomes quite acidotic and that can impair cardiac function, so to counter that, we'd given some bicarbonate.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So bicarbonate balances, did you say, the acid that builds up in the bloodstream?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. The acid builds up because of prolonged cardiac arrest, but the acid building up then impairs any effort to try and restart the heart. So the bicarbonate is to counter and get rid of the acid.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And it thereby adjusts the pH --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- of the blood?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Brings it back towards normal.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: One bolus of, is that...
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: 0.3ml of 10% -- that's calcium gluconate. Calcium is not often used in resuscitation anymore. It used to be common when I first trained. By [Baby C]'s time we weren't using it very often, but it's sometimes used as a last resort because giving an intravenous dose of calcium can sometimes help to restart a heart when other measures have failed.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Last resort because?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Because all the efforts we had done before with the ventilation and the cardiac compressions and multiple doses of different drugs and boluses had not restarted [Baby C]'s heart
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: and he'd not started to breathe again spontaneously. So the calcium was the last effort to try and restart his heart.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And then I think you then list, presumably, what you found having tried all of those methods.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Could you --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It says there "throughout" meaning during the whole time of his resuscitation. But to check the breathing, to check for a pulse, whether [Baby C] has got his own pulse or spontaneous breathing, you have to pause resuscitation for 5 or 10 seconds, not too long, to check will [Baby C] take a breath, has he got any pulse.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So it's only at intervals throughout the resuscitation we were checking for signs of life. But each time we checked for signs of life there was never any heart sounds heard -- that's after I arrived anyway -- there was no pulse felt, and no spontaneous respirations.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So where you put "no pulse" I think it says "when chest compressions stopped".
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That's what you're telling us: there's a pause, you check, and you go back to it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You keep pressing the chest regularly, sort of round about 100-120 times per minute, which means twice a second, really. You keep pressing the chest regularly, but every few minutes you ask people to stop resuscitation briefly to check does [Baby C] have a pulse.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Because when you're pressing the chest, you sometimes have a weak pulse because the idea of pressing the chest is to try and compress the heart and squirt some blood round the body, so you're producing an artificial pulse.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Next line is:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Cold light. No transillumination"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. It runs on a bit -- I'll explain what it means.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: It's:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Cold light. No transillumination suggestive of pneumothorax."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And pneumothorax is appearing on the line below because it runs off the page.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And a cold light is just a bright light that we shine against the chest of babies, although it's bright it's not hot, which is why it's called a cold light.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And that is a quick method of checking has a lung collapsed. So air has escaped from a lung which might have burst and air has escaped on the outside of the lung --
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. So that's a pneumothorax?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Pneumothorax, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So just tell us a little bit more, for the layperson amongst us, the -- so there's a burst in the lung?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: There can be a burst -- well, in the pneumothorax there's been a tear somewhere in the lung surface.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And what happens as a result of that tear?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Normally, the lungs fill the chest on either side and they reach out to the chest wall. If one of the lungs tears on its surface, air escapes out of the lungs, which could be roughly thought of as two large balloons.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Air escapes on the outside of the lung, collects inside the chest wall, but compresses the lung from outside and the lung collapses down completely because of the air on the outside of the lung.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So the lung would ordinarily fill the entire cavity?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: On each side, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The air escapes, starts to fill the cavity, thereby reducing the space (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, compressing the lung underneath. That needs a chest drain inserting to get the air out to allow the lung to reexpand.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Now, the only reason we're looking for that is because we were failing to save [Baby C]. We could not get him to breathe him again or his heart to restart and we were looking for unusual reasons why the resuscitation was failing, was unsuccessful. That's why we looked for a possible pneumothorax.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Why were you resorting to finding unusual reasons? Were things not progressing as you might have imagined?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: There's two answers to that. The first answer is, no, they weren't progressing as I'd expected because most babies who suddenly collapse, who have not been obviously very ill for some time beforehand, you would expect to respond to resuscitation. They may not all survive in the long term but it's unusual not to be able to restart the heart and to help the baby to regain some breaths if they have suddenly collapsed without a prolonged preceding illness.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. That's the first part. The second reason?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: When undertaking a prolonged resuscitation, giving breaths to [Baby C], because he wasn't breathing by himself with the Neopuff initially and then down the tube into his windpipe, inadvertently -- and it's just an adverse effect of having to ventilate someone -- you might rupture a lung by injecting gas under or squeezing gas under pressure into the lung. That could be compromising your ability to revive the patient because their lungs have collapsed. That's why we check for that possibility.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So you use the cold light to check for that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And briefly how does the cold light work? What would it show you if it was --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, you turn the lights out in the room -- you don't need to turn them all out but you need a dull light.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: When you shine the cold light against the chest wall, if there's no pneumothorax you don't see much at all, just a little bit of a brightness around where the light has been shone. If there's a pneumothorax, the whole side of the chest lights up like a lantern because that's the light radiating through the air on the outside of the lung.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So that space that's been created by the leak is illuminated?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, and that is called transillumination because it is illuminating through the chest. But it says there was no transillumination, so [Baby C] hadn't had a pneumothorax -- or at least if there was a pneumothorax it was very small and wouldn't be compromising the resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. Thank you. I think the next line probably refers back to what you were telling us earlier, is that US?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Ultrasound brain. No PVH seen."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: PVH is an abbreviation -- sorry, it's a long term.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Have the jury been told about periventricular haemorrhages?
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: They haven't, but just in laymen's terms for now, can you just tell us what you were ruling out?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Bleeds in the centre of the brain -- and I mentioned a little earlier that premature babies are prone to develop bleeds in the centre of the brain and this is -- they are called periventricular haemorrhages, so that's PVH.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But again, because [Baby C] had not responded as expected to these resuscitation measures, we were looking for other causes other problems that were compromising the resuscitation such as -- and it would have been a massive bleed inside his head for him not to have responded to resuscitation, but the ultrasound did not show any bleed.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So that one is ruled out as well. "No further"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Drugs.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. So:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "No further drugs or fluids given after 30 minutes."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And you have put a time there of 11.55?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Just explain that to us, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Here I'm recording the fact that resuscitation has failed and therefore we were not going to give any further drugs. We'd already given a large number of drugs as listed and discussed already.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And they'd failed to revive [Baby C] and he was showing no signs of life at this stage. Now, I'm sorry if it's misleading a bit, because I've thought about the timing.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I say after 30 minutes, I think the resuscitation had started around about 11.15. I wasn't there then. I was called just
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: before 11.30, I'd got there about 5, 6, 7 minutes later and the resuscitation continued for about 20 minutes after I arrived. But I knew it had been going on for about 20 minutes before I arrived.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Now, Dr Davis, who's given evidence, I believe, she was there very soon after the beginning of the resuscitation. So you can take her evidence of how long it had been going on before I arrived. So when I say 30 minutes, I think probably altogether all the efforts that Dr Davis and the nurses had been making for [Baby C] were probably more 40 minutes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Would the time be accurate, the 11.55?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Because when you decide you're going to stop resuscitation, you note the clock time because if you're stopping because resuscitation has failed, that would be the time when normally you'd record death --
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- but we didn't in [Baby C] for reasons that'll become apparent in a moment.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes. Your next line, I think, of your notes will explain what happened after 11.55.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. At that stage resuscitation had failed. It's usually recommended in various paediatric texts and manuals for resuscitation of babies and children that resuscitation can be stopped or should be stopped after around 20 minutes with no response. That's no heart restarting, no spontaneous breathing. It is very common in practice to continue longer than that just in the hope you might be able to save a baby.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So the fact this was 40 minutes altogether is not unusual. But that is much longer than is normally considered appropriate because if, after 20 minutes or so of proper resuscitation, you've not restarted the heart or got breathing going again, it is generally futile to continue because the heart will not restart and the breathing won't start again.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: This suggests, am I reading it right, "Continued chest compressions"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. We continued with a token resuscitation for [Baby C] because his parents wanted him christened and they did ask if he could be christened by both a Catholic priest and a Church of England minister. The Catholic priest had been called at some
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: stage during the resuscitation and he'd arrived by 11.55. The Anglican minister had not yet arrived.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right, okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And I don't know all the rules and regulations in the Church of England and the Roman Catholic Church but my understanding was christening or baptism is undertaken of a live patient and you shouldn't undertake it or it can't be undertaken after death, which is why we didn't officially say that [Baby C] was dead at 11.55 but carried on a token resuscitation waiting for his christening to then stop and check for signs of life to confirm he was dead.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. If we follow your note, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's just to read through that? So:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Continued chest compression and ventilation via the endotracheal tube [ETT]. Awaiting arrival of both Catholic priest and C of E vicar."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And I put in brackets:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Performed by Dr Katherine Davis and Staff Nurse Mel Taylor."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That means that the chest compressions and ventilation were carried on by Dr Davis and Staff Nurse Taylor:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Parents aware that resuscitation has been unsuccessful but we are awaiting [Baby C] to be christened before declaring him dead."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. Did you remain until such time as the christening or baptism had been completed?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Um... Yes. I can't remember what time I left the unit that night, but I was there until after the christening.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We've heard, as you have pointed out, from Dr Davis already, so we know that events continued into the early hours.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Can you tell us what you recall up until you left?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, surprisingly, while we were waiting for the two ministers of religion to turn up to do the christening, there were some signs of life that reappeared in [Baby C].
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I hadn't been expecting that. I was not sure initially what to do because we had stopped full resuscitation, we were only continuing a token form of resuscitation, just to allow [Baby C] to be christened before he was declared dead.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So really, I'm not sure why his breathing and a very feeble -well, occasional gasps of breathing and feeble heartbeats restarted at that stage. But they did and after discussion with [Baby C]'s parents, it was my view, and they agreed, that it was not appropriate to institute full resuscitation and try to revive him again, even though he was showing some fairly minimal signs of life. Because he hadn't shown signs of life for such a long time, the chance of him recovering, if we were able to salvage him at that stage, was remote.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The chance of him recovering without profound brain damage was extremely remote, so no further vigorous resuscitation was initiated at that stage.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. If we just finish your note, please, I think that may cover --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We got as far as Dr Katherine Davis and Nurse Taylor?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Parents aware resuscitation has been unsuccessful.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Between 11.55 and 00.30, intermittent gasps but no heart sounds or spontaneous pulse."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Then I've signed it and put my name in capitals.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I should add, though, that later on that night, heart sounds were heard, I don't know about a pulse.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Dr Davis might have informed you of that. I was writing this -at the beginning of this entry it says 00.30.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I think the christening hadn't taken place at that stage, we were still waiting for the Anglican minister to turn up. But some time after that, the heart sounds were heard.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: All right. We heard from Dr Davis that you then left in the early hours of the morning.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What was the situation, can you recall, when you left the unit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: After the christening, which was probably 50 minutes after the full resuscitation had been stopped, so nearly an hour afterwards, the intention was to declare [Baby C] dead then having been christened. But because he was showing these residual signs of life, gasping, respirations, a feeble heartbeat, he wasn't dead. But we planned to offer just palliative care, just to keep him comfortable because he was dying basically. But it was 5 hours after the christening that finally no heartbeat was heard and no further gasping respirations.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We heard that even once you had gone home you were contacted I think on two occasions?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And asked about --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't remember how many occasions.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You were certainly contacted again and asked about medications; do you recall that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Firstly, we didn't expect [Baby C] to show any signs of life after we stopped full resuscitation. Then even though he did, I expected those to stop fairly soon, but Dr Katherine Davis phoned me, I can't remember how many times -- if it was twice I don't dispute that -- to say that [Baby C] is still showing breathing efforts and heartbeats. We weren't feeding him, we had stopped the intravenous fluids, he wasn't getting any nutrition, and he would have been getting dehydrated during that stage.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: It's very difficult to know what a 30-weeker feels anyway. We wouldn't know whether [Baby C] was in distress but I know that he would be getting dehydrated and hungry if we weren't giving him fluids and therefore it was appropriate to give him some morphine to relieve any distress, which is part of palliative care management.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You didn't have any more dealings with [Baby C] that particular shift that morning?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not that I recall.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. I think your next, if I can use this term, involvement came later in the day. If we can go, please, to slide 271, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we scroll down the note. I am sure I can take the liberty of simply reading this: at 1.30 that afternoon you called the
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: coroner's office and you left a message on the answerphone to notify them of presumably [Baby C]'s death?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, because it was an unexpected and unexplained death, so he was referred to the coroner because I couldn't provide a cause for death.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We've heard that in the event of a death of a baby on the unit, there would often be a debrief --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- that would take place some time afterwards?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Could we go next to 308?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We have here, Dr Gibbs, your note of that debrief.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We can see 2 July 2015.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Which is just over 2 weeks after [Baby C]'s sad death. It took 2 weeks, as it often does. A debrief ought to be carried out soon after any major event, but it does depend on the various people involved at the time of the event all being on duty again because they're working different shifts. It doesn't mean everyone who was involved gets to the debrief but usually those at the debrief are at least some of the people involved in the incident for which the debrief is being held.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: If I can take you through the names. Eirian Powell?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: She's the ward manager, the most senior nurse on the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: She wasn't on duty at the time [Baby C] died, but being the senior nurse she's there to support her nursing colleagues, so she tends to attend debriefing sessions .
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. And I'd hope the remainder of the names are people we've already heard from: Mel Taylor, Katherine Davis, Sophie Ellis, yourself and, of course, Lucy Letby.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Can you take us through the note, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right. I say that -- I've written that:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Discussed the events leading up to [Baby C]'s 'arrest".
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I put "arrest" in single quotation marks simply because that's what we call a sudden collapse, a seeming loss of any breathing and circulation, no heart beating or very slow heartbeat. Then I put little dashes here as points:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Did not seem unwell."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Meaning [Baby C] didn't appear unwell beforehand.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We were not expecting to have a cardiorespiratory arrest:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "He had been active."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Then I put down:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Kept pulling out NG tubes."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Bear in mind I'm just recording what we've discussed in this debrief. This isn't a note for the debrief, this is a summary of the debrief. So this would be everyone involved in the debrief's views, so I'd imagine pulling out the nasogastric tube was something I was told by the nurses. But it just meant he was an active little baby.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: CRP is a C-reactive protein.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We've heard about that, thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And the white cell count had suggested infection but was on -- this is where -- sorry, I've reached the end of the line. I put the word "antibiotics" underneath it with a little half square around it. It should read:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "CRP and white cell count suggested infection but was on antibiotics."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: He'd been on antibiotics for several days.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Then the fourth entry, please, "not related"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Not related to 0.5ml feed."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I think I was trying to write something and crossed it out and then put "feed". So not related to 0.5ml feed. Little [Baby C], we'd been holding off his feeds because he was at risk of possibly developing necrotising enterocolitis, and feeding can precipitate necrotising enterocolitis if you start it too soon in a baby prone to that condition. But we had that evening -- I said we had, I had in the morning from the notes we've already looked at, Sally Ogden, the registrar, had written down that I
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: had suggested that if his aspirates didn't get any larger, then we could start some trophic feeds. That's a small amount of feed. The 0.5ml was the feed that was started because his gastric aspirates hadn't worsened. But that feed was given shortly before his cardiorespiratory arrest.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We have heard from Nurse Ellis who dealt with that.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't understand how 0.5ml of feed would ever cause a cardiorespiratory arrest, that's why we're saying it's not related to that. The reason to put that down is obviously the nurses felt very bad that they had just given him a feed -- and it wasn't instantly, it was a few minutes later, maybe up to 15 minutes later, he had his cardiac arrest.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The nurses felt bad about it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Because they'd given the feed. I had said that he could be fed, but if you're the person that gives the feed and you wonder, did that cause him a problem, you would feel bad about having given the feed.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Of course, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: But the feed did not cause -- was not related to his cardiorespiratory arrest, in my opinion, in any way.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is that "discussed resuscitation"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Discussed resuscitation. Technically performed well. Team worked well together."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And the reason we discussed this -- it sounds we're all congratulating ourselves and poor little [Baby C] is dead. When a tragedy happens and we lose a patient we always ask ourselves could we have done anything about it, could we have predicted this, and could we have managed the resuscitation any differently or better.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And the feeling from this debrief, that is it was our views, is that we'd done everything we could and we'd resuscitated him well, sadly unsuccessfully.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: There's a dash after "together". Is it "causes"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, "Causes of PEA", that's another abbreviation. It stands for pulseless electrical activity. That's a form of cardiac arrest. It's when the heart is not beating, there's no pulse, so there is no circulation, so effectively you are dead
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: if your heart is not beating, but you can still see some electrical impulses on a monitor. That just means electricity is circulating around the heart like it's supposed to from the pacemaker, but the heart is not being or pumping any blood. It's a form of cardiac arrest.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: But I was saying:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Causes of cardiac arrest considered and their management."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So the different causes. And we had during the resuscitation thought about different causes of cardiac arrest, including this particular pulseless electrical activity, PEA, and we'd not been able to find them or we had given treatment to counter any of those causes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But I'm saying here:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "[Although] [that's an abbreviation for although] it's not possible to exclude pulmonary [so lung] a pulmonary embolus or toxins at the time of the resuscitation."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What's a pulmonary embolus?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's usually due to a blood clot which has developed somewhere in the body. It's rare in babies and children, it's more common in adults where you get a blood clot developing in one of the legs and you hear of that happening in people who haven't moved their legs for a long time on a long haul flight get blood clots in the leg. That's called a deep venous thrombosis, a DVT.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But a blood clot can sometimes break off from elsewhere in the body, pass through the circulation, get into the lungs and block the circulation in the lungs. And that would lead to a cardiac arrest.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Was this debrief taking place before or after the postmortem?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Before the post-mortem -- no, the post-mortem had been held, this is 2 weeks after, but none of us knew the results of the post-mortem.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You go on to -- you say:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Not possible to exclude toxins at the time of resuscitation."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: What did you have in mind there?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: One of the rare causes of cardiac arrest that does not respond to the usual measures is that some poisoning has occurred. This is more common in older children, toddlers particularly, who have come across a parent's or grandparent's medication, think it's sweets, ingested the medication, and because it's an adult size dose that a little child has taken, some medications can have a severe adverse effect on the heart and cause cardiac arrest. So it's a massive toxin overdose.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We've heard about excluding various things. These are thoughts being had before the results of the post-mortem had been received?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. These are causes where resuscitation has been unsuccessful, what might have caused it. Well, a pulmonary embolus -- if the lungs are completely blocked with the clot you can't get the circulation restarted during resuscitation. If a patient has been severely poisoned sometimes all your efforts to restart the heart and breathing will be unsuccessful.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. The next line makes it clear that the post-mortem results are not yet available. Can we carry on, "following"? "Following decision" is it? If we can scroll down a little.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Following decision to stop active resuscitation after 25 minutes..."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And I have to apologise, this is why I say the timing -- I say 30 minutes previously, I say 25 minutes here. It depends on whether you are timing it from when Dr Davis and the nurses started it or when I arrived at 25 to. So there's a difference. But the total resuscitation, full resuscitation, was 40 minutes. But it was about 20 or 25 minutes after I had arrived, which is why I say 25 minutes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Following the decision to stop active resuscitation after 25 minutes [because there was no pulse or respiration at that stage], ventilation and gentle chest compressions continued for another 50 minutes simply to allow baptism before formally and legally declaring [Baby C] dead."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is that "unfortunately"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry. Unfortunately, there was a delay. And it's something I've already mentioned:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "A delay in the Church of England vicar arriving (the Catholic priest arrived before the end of active resuscitation) and the
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: parents wanted baptism by a C of E vicar, then blessing by a Catholic priest. By the end of the baptism, which was 40 minutes after we stopped the active resuscitation, [Baby C] had a pulse and intermittent gasping respirations. But agreed with parents that further life support measures were futile.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: [Baby C] showed some signs of life for the next 5 hours whilst being cuddled by parents."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I wasn't there for all of that, but this is from the debrief, so various nurses and Dr Davis, who had been involved, would have reported that.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And if we can scroll down again, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It was an unusual situation to prolong token resuscitation after stopping proper resuscitation, but I did it in the best interests, I felt, at that time, to allow a christening by the two ministers of religion.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But I think everyone who had been involved felt uncomfortable that [Baby C]'s heart and breathing had restarted at a stage when it was futile to continue any further, and we thought in future we would try and avoid this situation. So, in future, once active resuscitation stops, if no minister of religion is available, baptism should be performed by a member of staff rather than prolonging a token resuscitation that risks revitalising the brain, the brainstem functions, in an otherwise profoundly hypoxic ischaemic impaired infant. That means an infant who's suffered severe lack of circulation to all their body organs.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: This is a view going forward based on what --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- had happened?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, to try and avoid the situation of waiting for 40 minutes for ministers of religion to arrive. The situation of two ministers of religion being involved and parents wishing to wait for the second one to arrive who is delayed is unusual, but the principle of stopping resuscitation when felt to be futile should be followed.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Having said that's what we should do, the reason I put the next bit in capitals is a final decision hadn't been made because that's myself discussing it with some of the people involved in the resuscitation, with the ward manager there as well, (inaudible: coughing) hadn't(?) been discussed with the rest of the consultants in the department, and we take team decisions
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: when we're changing policy. So, however, I will discuss with consultant colleagues.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right. Then we can see again your signature --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- in the bottom corner.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: But discussions with the consultant colleagues -- they all readily agreed we should follow this policy of not waiting for a minister of religion to arrive if we decide a child is dead to actually -- for someone on the unit to christen the child themselves.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. If we can come out, please, and go to the next tile, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This is described as a SUDIC strategy meeting.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: What's that, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: SUDIC is an abbreviation for sudden unexpected death in infancy. So any child who dies unexpectedly, which applies to many children's deaths -- if a child is being treated for cancer and is getting worse and is unresponsive to further treatment and then dies, that's an expected death. But a SUDIC means the death wasn't expected and they all have to be investigated.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So these are the minutes of that meeting. If we scroll down, please, it's there for anyone to read at a later stage. If we scroll down, we can see [Baby C]'s name.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I have no more questions for you, Dr Gibbs.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Am I allowed to add another point?
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Of course you can.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's a point I want to make because I'm aware that repeatedly I've said that [Baby C]'s parents wanted both ministers of religion to be there to christen him and that's why we continued a token, not a proper, resuscitation, waiting for the second minister to turn up. And it sort of implies, one might think, and the parents might think I'm blaming them that we had to wait for the other minister of religion to come. It's not their fault. The fault is that [Baby C]'s heart and breathing restarted again and that should never have happened. If you've had an unsuccessful resuscitation after 40 minutes of full resuscitation, the national guidelines are that you
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: shouldn't continue for more than 20 minutes because it's futile if you haven't restarted the heart.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I can't imagine, can't think of any natural disease process that would allow a heart to restart later on when you hadn't been able to get that heart to restart with full intensive care and multiple doses of adrenaline and so on. So that suggests, and I can't say any more than that, I don't know what it was, that whatever catastrophic event led to his death was reversing or had reversed after we stopped resuscitation. I don't understand that from a natural disease process.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So it was quite reasonable for [Baby C]'s parents to request that we waited -- well, we christened him. It was a shame that it just took a bit of time for the two ministers of religion to both turn up. It was my decision that we carry on this token resuscitation so we would delay certifying [Baby C] dead until the ministers arrived. The problem was, his heart should not have restarted, he shouldn't have started breathing again, and that's the difficulty. So I'm not trying to say it went a bit wrong and we prolonged [Baby C]'s death because the parents wanted the two ministers to christen him.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. I'm told there was a technical hiccup, so we can now, my Lord, go back to the form that was on the screen.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: If we just go to box 2, please, Dr Gibbs. This was your contribution to the inquiry that was made:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Dr Gibbs stated that [Baby C] was born at 30 weeks gestation. Labour was induced due to poor in utero growth and his birth weight was 800 grams, which was half the expected weight of a baby for that gestational period. [Baby C] looked normal at birth. He was very small. The cause of the poor growth is as yet unknown.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: He was initially ventilated for his first few hours and then he managed on Optiflow with 25% oxygen over the next few days. He was generally managing well and there were no concerns."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that --
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I think that's correct. I think to be absolutely accurate, he was ventilated for the first few hours, then he went on to CPAP, which I think the jury have been told about.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And then he went on to Optiflow. It looks here as though he only had Optiflow afterwards, but I think that detail's just missing.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes, we've been through that sequence. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Due to having a high risk of developing necrotising enterocolitis (which is common in very premature babies) [Baby C] was not given his first milk feed until he was 4 days old. [Baby C] was given 0.5ml nasogastrically and it was shortly after this feed that he collapsed. The feeding tube had been inserted correctly and if milk had got into his lungs, such a small amount would have caused minimal problems. Oxygen saturates dropped and there was no pulse [of] heart rate traced."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Pulse or heart rate", yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "CPR was started immediately following his collapse.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The registrar arrived within 1 minute and attempted to intubate but was unable to do so and CPR continued.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: During this time there was good chest movement. After 10 minutes, the consultant was successful in intubating and there was no sign of milk present in the windpipe and [Baby C]'s lungs were clear. Resuscitation continued for a further 25 minutes, during which time [Baby C] received eight doses of IV adrenaline, saline volume expansion boluses, bicarbonate, a bolus of glucose and a final bolus of calcium. [Baby C] did not respond to resuscitation. He took no breaths and there was no heartbeat or pulse. His mum was present throughout and his dad arrived during resuscitation. It was agreed that it was futile to continue with resuscitation as [Baby C] had suffered severe hypoxic ischaemic encephalopathy.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The parents requested that [Baby C] be baptised by both a Catholic priest and Anglican priest in keeping with both parents' religions. The Catholic priest arrived a few minutes before it was agreed to stop resuscitation but the Anglican priest could attend for up to an hour as she had to travel from the Wirral."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Presumably "could not attend":
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "It was agreed to continue with gentle chest compressions and some oxygen but that no further drugs would be administered. During this further period on resuscitation (50 minutes) there was a pulse present and the baby took a few gasping breaths. [Baby C] showed residual signs of life with no recovery and parents agreed that it was futile to continue once baptism had
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: taken place. Resuscitation was stopped and [Baby C] was given to his parents to cuddle. [Baby C] died 5 hours later in his parents' arms. The case was discussed with the coroner and it was agreed that a post-mortem would be undertaken to ascertain the cause of death."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's your entry on -- your contribution to the meeting.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Which is summarising [Baby C]'s --
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes, thank you. They are all the questions, Dr Gibbs, I have for you. Thank you, if you could wait there.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, you'll be some time?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I will be, my Lord, yes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I think just for the sake of completeness, severe hypoxic ischaemic encephalopathy is?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Right. Well, encephalopathy --
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We don't need a medical lecture, but basically if you can break it down as simply as possible.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Profound brain damage due to lack of blood and oxygen reaching the brain, which would also affect all other organs in the body.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: There we are. Thank you. We'll break off there. Thank you very much, Dr Gibbs. I'm afraid it's not been possible to complete your evidence, but looking at the chart that I have, you're going to be attending quite a few more times, it is likely. Thank you very much. You obviously know that you're in the middle of your evidence and not to talk to anyone about anything to do with this case and the evidence you've given.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much. Could you be ready, please, to resume at 10.30 tomorrow morning? Thank you very much, doctor. Either stay for the moment or leave as you wish.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (Pause)

Thank you very much. Would you please make what enquiries you can, those of you who travel by train and are reliant on train for getting to this courtroom, what the situation is going to be on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday? And is it Thursday? And Thursday. Because I think Monday and Wednesday are strike days, but there are expected to be knock-on effects on Tuesday and Thursday because of the strikes. And what other possible alternative arrangements you may be able to make or not as the
case may be so that we'll know tomorrow, or certainly Wednesday, how we're going to deal with the plan for next week. All right? Thank you very much.
And as far as you're concerned, you may be assured that that will be accommodated.
(In the absence of the jury)
Sorry, I didn't wish to sound rude, Dr Gibbs, when I said I don't want a medical lecture. You in fact summarised it very clearly and very concisely, for which I'm grateful.
I took the hint, thank you.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: No, no, they're terms with which I'm familiar, but I just wanted to make sure it was in evidence for the jury. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I don't know whether anyone else is going to be affected by these strikes or not, but if anyone is, we will discuss the arrangements. I'm thinking of witnesses as well who may be scheduled for that time and may have difficulty and so on and so forth. But I think we ought to try and make sure this is resolved on Wednesday if possible or Wednesday and Thursday and certainly not leave it until Friday. But from your point of view, the earlier the better.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The court adjourned until 10.30 am on Tuesday, 1 November 2022)
